title: A conversation
hook: a sacred hadith says Allah answers each line of the Fatiha as it is said (Muslim)

segments.voice: Yesterday: seven verses, said seventeen times a day. Your line was the most repeated words. Did you count, and which time felt most awake? Day three hundred thirty-four.

There's a kind of phone call where you talk and nobody answers. Voicemail. You say your piece into the quiet, hang up, and hope it lands. Prayer can sound like that from the outside: words going out, silence coming back. Sahih Muslim preserves a hadith that pictures the Fatiha very differently. In it, every line the worshipper says gets a reply, right then, before the next line starts. Not voicemail. A conversation. Today we listen to both sides of it.
screen: `WORDS INTO THE QUIET.` → `WHAT IF EVERY LINE GOT A REPLY?` → `BOTH SIDES OF THE FATIHA.`

segments.voice: This is a hadith qudsi, a sacred hadith: words the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ reported from God Himself, but which are not part of the Qur'an. It's in Sahih Muslim. God says: I have divided the prayer between Myself and My servant into two halves, and My servant will have what he asks. Then it walks through the surah. The servant says: praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds. And God says: My servant has praised Me. The servant says: the Beneficent, the Merciful. God says: My servant has extolled Me. The servant says: Owner of the Day of Judgment. God says: My servant has glorified Me. Then the hinge, the middle verse: Thee alone we worship, Thee alone we ask for help. And God says: this is between Me and My servant, and My servant will have what he asked. Then the last lines, show us the straight path, and God says: this is for My servant, and My servant will have what he asked. Notice the shape. The first half belongs to God: praise. The middle is shared. The last half belongs to the person: a request. And every line gets an answer. One detail stands out. In this hadith, the replies aren't promised for a perfect recitation; they're described as coming each time the line is said. That's why some teachers tell people to pause a breath after each verse. Not because the reply needs time. Because the one praying needs a moment to remember there is one. He answers each line.
screen: `A SACRED HADITH, IN SAHIH MUSLIM` · `MY SERVANT HAS PRAISED ME` · `THE MIDDLE VERSE IS SHARED` · `PAUSE: THERE IS A REPLY`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pause after each line. Say the Fatiha now, aloud or silently, in Arabic or in English. After each verse, stop for one breath. In that breath, you can recall the reply from the hadith: praised, extolled, glorified, between Me and My servant, for My servant. If you don't pray, simply listen to the gaps between the lines, and notice how different the words feel with space around them. The bell holds the time.
A conversation. The Fatiha as two voices: the worshipper speaks a line, and in the sacred hadith God answers it, half praise, half request, the middle shared. Today's word.
Your line: he answers each line. Today, in one prayer or one quiet minute, leave a breath of space after each verse. Day three hundred thirty-four.

howItsDone: Many Muslims recite al-Fatiha slowly, pausing at the end of each verse; teachers often cite the hadith qudsi in Sahih Muslim, in which God answers each line, as the reason for the pause.

fork.setup: you reach the middle verse: Thee alone we worship, Thee alone we ask for help. in the hadith, whose verse is it?
options: shared between God and the servant.
fork.reveal: shared: this is between Me and My servant. worship faces God, asking for help faces the person, and the verse holds both.

what a scholar hears: Sahih Muslim's hadith qudsi of the divided prayer, which scholars also cite in the debate over whether the bismillah is part of the Fatiha, since the hadith begins at praise be to Allah.

notes: Sahih Muslim 395 cited from memory; the replies (praised, extolled, glorified; between Me and My servant; for My servant) are paraphrased. Please confirm wording and number. Some narrations add 'My servant has entrusted his affairs to Me' at the Day of Judgment line; omitted for length.
Trapdoor: the hadith beginning at 'praise be to Allah' is cited in fiqh discussions about whether the bismillah is a verse of the Fatiha (a Maliki/Hanafi argument); confirm this is a fair summary.
The pause after each verse: also supported by a report of the Prophet reciting verse by verse (Abu Dawud, Tirmidhi); not cited in the script.
